notes.meaning: Paul began his speech by addressing the angry crowd as his brothers and fathers. He was not apologizing for doing wrong, but offering a reasoned defense of his life and actions. Even though they had just attacked him, he treated them with courtesy and respect.

When the people heard Paul speaking to them in their own local language, Aramaic, the crowd quieted down even more. They may have expected a Greek-speaking rebel who despised Jewish ways, so his familiar words caught their attention. Speaking their mother tongue showed his deep respect for them and bought him a quiet hearing.

Paul established his Jewish background by explaining that he was born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem. He studied under Gamaliel, the most respected Jewish teacher of that era, and was trained strictly in the law of their ancestors. He understood their passion because he once had that exact same burning zeal for God.

Paul confessed that he had fiercely persecuted the early Christians, referred to here as 'this Way.' He had arrested both men and women without pity and put them into prison, seeking their deaths. Sharing his harsh past showed that only a real act of God could have changed his heart.

Paul pointed out that the current high priest and the entire Jewish council could confirm his story. In those days, they had given him official letters authorizing him to travel to Damascus. His mission was to arrest believers there and bring them back to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.

As Paul came close to Damascus around midday, a dazzling light from heaven suddenly flashed all around him. Because this happened under the bright noon sun, it was far more brilliant than daylight. It showed clearly that something supernatural from God was breaking into his life.

The blinding flash of light threw Paul flat on the ground in shock. Then he heard a heavenly voice calling his name twice to get his full attention. The voice asked him directly why he was persecuting Him.

Paul asked who was speaking, and the voice replied, 'I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.' Paul suddenly realized that the crucified Jesus was alive in heavenly glory. In attacking the followers of Jesus, Paul was actually attacking the Lord Himself.

The men traveling with Paul saw the bright light and were terrified, but they could not understand the voice speaking to him. They heard a sound or noise, but only Paul received the distinct words. The message was intended specifically for Paul's heart and calling.

Paul surrendered immediately, asking what the Lord wanted him to do. Jesus told him to stand up and continue into Damascus, where he would receive his instructions. God chose to use a human messenger in the city to guide the new convert into his appointed work.

The intense brightness of the heavenly light left Paul completely blind. His traveling companions had to lead him by the hand the rest of the way into Damascus. The once-proud persecutor entered the city humbled and physically helpless.

In Damascus, God sent a man named Ananias to visit Paul. Ananias was a faithful follower of Jesus who also strictly observed the Jewish law and was well respected by all the local Jews. Paul highlighted this to prove that his teacher was not an enemy of Israel's traditions.

Ananias came to Paul's side and greeted him warmly as 'Brother Saul,' telling him to receive his sight. At that very moment, Paul was completely healed and could look up and see him. This miracle confirmed that Ananias had truly been sent by the Lord.

Ananias told Paul that the God of their Jewish ancestors had chosen him beforehand. God's purpose was for Paul to know His divine will, see the Righteous One (Jesus Christ), and hear His voice directly. This direct revelation gave Paul the special qualification needed to be an apostle.

God appointed Paul to be an official witness for Christ to all people everywhere. He was called to tell both Jews and Gentiles what he had personally seen and heard. Sharing his own story would help persuade others to trust in the Savior.

Ananias urged Paul not to delay, but to rise, receive baptism, and have his sins washed away as he called on the name of the Lord. In the Christian life, baptism is the outward sign of entering into Christ's family and receiving forgiveness. True spiritual cleansing comes through calling on Jesus in faith.

differ.view: Baptists teach that baptism does not wash away sins, but is an outward picture of the spiritual washing and salvation that a believer has already received through faith in Christ.
Presbyterians and Reformed believers teach that baptism is an outward sign and seal of the inward forgiveness of sins that Christ's blood provides, rather than the mechanical cause of cleansing.
Methodists teach that baptism is both an appointed means and seal of pardon for true penitents, which God ordinarily used in the early church to convey forgiveness.

notes.meaning: Paul recounted that about three years later, he returned to Jerusalem and went to pray in the temple. While praying there, he fell into a trance or spiritual vision. Praying in the temple showed that he still honored it as God's holy place of worship.

In this vision, Paul saw Jesus commanding him to leave Jerusalem in a hurry. The Lord warned him that the people in the city would not accept his testimony about Christ. God knew their hearts would remain hard against the gospel.

Paul tried to reason with the Lord, thinking the people in Jerusalem would naturally listen to him. They knew well that he had once hunted down believers and had them beaten in the synagogues. Paul felt his sudden turn to Christ was such powerful evidence that no one could ignore it.

Paul reminded the Lord of his role in the death of Stephen, the first Christian martyr. He had stood by approving of the murder and guarding the coats of the men throwing the stones. Remembering his terrible past kept Paul humble, but he thought it would make his witness even more convincing to the Jews.

Jesus overruled Paul's argument and gave him a clear command to go. The Lord told him that his mission was not in Jerusalem, but far away among the Gentiles (non-Jewish nations). Paul wanted the crowd to see that preaching to Gentiles was God's direct command, not his own personal choice.

The crowd listened patiently until Paul mentioned being sent to the Gentiles. At that word, they erupted into wild fury, shouting that such a man should be wiped off the earth because he did not deserve to live. They were deeply offended by the idea that non-Jewish people could share equally in God's promises.

The mob flew into an uncontrolled rage, shouting, tearing off their outer clothes, and throwing handfuls of dust into the air. These actions showed their fierce hatred and their readiness to stone Paul on the spot if they could reach him. Because Roman soldiers protected him, throwing dirt was their only way to vent their fury.

The Roman commander ordered Paul to be taken inside the military fortress for his own safety. Since he did not understand Aramaic, he did not know why the crowd had exploded into such anger. He decided to have Paul whipped and questioned, assuming he must have committed a terrible crime to cause such a riot.

As the soldiers stretched Paul out and tied him with leather straps to be flogged, Paul asked the nearby centurion if it was lawful to whip an uncondemned Roman citizen. Roman law strictly forbade beating a citizen who had not been tried and convicted of a crime. Paul used his legal rights wisely to prevent an unjust and brutal beating.

When the centurion heard Paul's question, he went straight to the commander to warn him. He urged the commander to think carefully about what he was doing because Paul was a Roman citizen. Violating a citizen's rights was a major offense that could cost Roman officers their ranks or lives.

The commander hurried over to Paul to verify the claim for himself, asking if he was truly a Roman citizen. Paul gave a direct and confident answer that he was. Falsely claiming Roman citizenship carried the death penalty, so the commander took his answer very seriously.

The commander remarked that it had cost him a huge amount of money to buy his Roman citizenship. Paul replied that he was actually born a citizen, which gave him an even higher legal status than the commander. Paul's family had likely received this valuable status generations earlier for service to the Roman state.

The soldiers who were about to whip and question Paul backed away at once. The commander himself became frightened when he realized he had illegally tied up a Roman citizen for torture. Fear of Roman law brought a sudden halt to their mistreatment of God's servant.

The next day, the commander still wanted to find out the real charges against Paul. He released Paul from his bonds and ordered the Jewish chief priests and the entire Sanhedrin (the high council) to hold an official meeting. He then brought Paul down to stand before them so the case could be examined properly.
